newsitem.title: USA: Snoring disorder linked to car accidents.
newsitem.headline: Snoring disorder linked to car accidents.

text.p: Habitual snorers who get behind the wheel during their waking hours may be at greater risk for car accidents due to fatigue, researchers said on Wednesday.

Snoring is often a sign of a condition known as sleep apnea, in which a person momentarily stops breathing several times throughout the night. Each time the breathing pauses, the person's sleep is broken, leading to severe daytime fatigue and cardiovascular problems.

Researchers at the University of Wisconsin Medical School said they found people with mild sleep apnea were three times more likely to be involved in car accidents than people who did not have the problem. People with moderate sleep apnea were seven times more likely to get into accidents.
In its mild form, sleep apnea is characterised by about five breathing pauses per hour of sleep, a number that can go up to almost 100 in some people.
Results of the University of Wisconsin study, which looked at the five-year driving records of 913 adults, were presented at the American Thoracic Society/American Lung Association conference here.
Sleep apnea is most prevalent in men, who are 2.5 times more likely than women to have the condition.
